big_idea: Feedback conversations fail not because managers lack good intentions but because they skip a step: figuring out which of three things the other person actually needs, appreciation, coaching, or evaluation, before speaking.

tool.label: The Three Types of Feedback (Appreciation / Coaching / Evaluation)
tool.text: Huston argues most people conflate all feedback into one bucket, but employees are actually asking for one of three distinct things: appreciation, recognition that their effort was seen; coaching, concrete suggestions to improve; or evaluation, where they stand against a standard. Before giving feedback, ask which of these three the person is looking for and match your delivery to the answer; giving evaluation when someone wanted appreciation, or vice versa, is a primary reason feedback lands badly.
tool.note: Huston recommends appreciation weekly, coaching regularly, and evaluation at least twice a year, not just at annual review time.

ideas.title: Listening before speaking
ideas.text: Effective feedback starts with understanding what kind of input the person is seeking, not with rehearsing what you plan to say.

ideas.title: State your good intent
ideas.text: Explicitly naming a constructive intention up front reduces defensiveness before the substance of the feedback arrives.

ideas.title: Critique the behavior, not the person
ideas.text: Framing feedback around specific actions and their impact, rather than character, keeps the conversation about something changeable.

ideas.title: Avoid why questions
ideas.text: Questions like why did you do that tend to trigger defensiveness rather than reflection; Huston suggests alternative phrasing that invites problem-solving.

ideas.title: Let the receiver talk back
ideas.text: Good feedback conversations leave room for the other person to correct inaccuracies or add context, rather than being one-way pronouncements.

ideas.title: Model receiving feedback publicly
ideas.text: Leaders who visibly share feedback they've gotten and what they're doing about it make it safer for others to hear and act on feedback too.

try_it: Before your next feedback conversation, ask the person directly: are you looking for appreciation, coaching, or an honest read on where you stand?
Rewrite one piece of planned feedback to remove any why question and replace it with a specific, observable behavior.
State your positive intent out loud in the first sentence of your next difficult feedback conversation.
Schedule one appreciation-only check-in this week with someone you usually only coach or evaluate.
best_for: Managers who dread or avoid giving feedback and want a low-friction way to start
Anyone whose feedback keeps landing wrong despite good intentions
less_useful: Readers looking for a research-heavy academic treatment rather than an accessible, anecdote-driven management guide
Teams where the core problem is a lack of any feedback culture at all rather than technique

related.why: A closely related framework combining direct challenge with genuine care in feedback
A complementary listening-based approach for change conversations that resist direct feedback

sources.label: ASCD, Therese Huston on Giving Better Feedback
